era_visual_canon.clothing: Miners wore utilitarian work clothes, likely denim or cotton overalls, heavy-duty shirts, work boots, hard hats, and rudimentary dust masks or cloth coverings. Civilian residents wore typical Australian outback attire of the period: light cotton shirts, shorts, trousers, and sundresses for women, with wide-brimmed hats for sun protection. Government officials wore suits and formal attire.
era_visual_canon.technology: Early 20th century industrial mining equipment, basic ventilation systems, conveyer belts, crushers, and grinders for asbestos processing. Diesel-powered machinery, analog gauges. Landline telephones, basic radios, manual typewriters. No advanced automation, digital displays, modern electronic control systems, computers, internet, or mobile phones.
era_visual_canon.vehicles_machinery: Heavy-duty mining trucks, bulldozers, and excavators typical of 1940s-1960s mining operations. Civilian vehicles included sedans and utility vehicles (utes) from Australian, American, and European manufacturers of the 1950s and 1960s, often dusty and weathered. Small propeller planes were used for transport to the remote location.
era_visual_canon.interiors: Simple, functional interiors in workers' housing, often constructed with readily available materials, including asbestos waste. Furnishings were basic and practical, likely timber or metal. Government and office interiors featured wooden desks, manual typewriters, and filing cabinets. Interiors would have visible dust accumulation from the pervasive asbestos.
era_visual_canon.forbidden_anachronisms: smartphones, LED screens, contemporary clothing, modern flat panels, digital watches, modern industrial safety equipment (e.g., advanced respirators, sealed suits), post-1970s vehicles, contemporary heavy machinery, modern clean energy infrastructure, GPS devices, ubiquitous modern plastics, satellite dishes.
era_visual_canon.materials_textures: corrugated iron, wood, fiber cement (uralite containing asbestos), reddish-brown earth/dust, blue asbestos tailings. Textures are weathered, dusty, rough, crumbling, friable, loose particulate matter, and sun-baked.
era_visual_canon.color_palette: exterior: muted reds, ochres, and browns from the desert earth and dust; weathered blue-grey of asbestos materials; dull metallic tones of corrugated iron. interior: faded pale colors, dusty off-whites, and natural tones of wood.
era_visual_canon.scale_dimensions: Small, isolated desert town, individual buildings are typically single-story or low-rise structures. The overall area is described as a vast zone, officially 46,840 hectares.
era_visual_canon.distinctive_features: An isolated Australian ghost town, visibly constructed with insidious blue asbestos waste from the 1937-1966 mining era, now a vast, toxic forbidden zone, characterized by a remote, desolate desert setting where pervasive asbestos tailings cover all structures, roads, and open spaces, creating a perpetually dusty and hazardous environment.
era_visual_canon.demographics: The population was composed of Australian and European migrants (notably Spanish from 1958) and displaced persons. Miners wore heavy-duty work clothes. Other residents wore typical 1950s-1960s Australian outback casual attire.
era_visual_canon.visual_reference_availability: Photographic records and textual descriptions from reports and personal accounts confirm the appearance of buildings (corrugated iron, wood), the dusty environment, the use of asbestos tailings in town construction, and the general state of the area. Specific details on clothing and technology are derived from historical context and documented roles.

condition_evolution.at_event: During its operational years (1937-1966), the town was active with mining operations, functioning buildings, roads, and a transient population. However, it was already characterized by pervasive asbestos dust covering workers, buildings, and the environment, as evidenced by contemporary reports.
condition_evolution.later: Post-1978, the town transitioned into a deserted ghost town. Buildings were progressively demolished (1986-1992, 2022-2023), services disconnected (2006), and its official status abolished (2007). It remains a vast, contaminated, and forbidden zone, with asbestos tailings actively eroding and spreading, confirmed by later environmental reports and ongoing legal actions.

periods.clothing: Miners in heavy-duty work clothes, hard hats, basic dust masks. Civilians in light cotton casual wear, wide-brimmed hats. Children in simple play clothes.
